findings.evidence: Approval Timeline: "The manager confirms the equipment category matches the approved list." Required Documentation: "The manager approves items pursuant to internal discretion." Program Coordination: "The team then routes the request to the correct approver based on department." Review Responsibility: "The finance office reviews every stipend request over 200 dollars before it pays out."
findings.fix: Replace the four separate accounts with one description of the approval chain, naming each role once, the order the roles act in, and the condition (if any) that brings each one in.
findings.location: Approval Timeline; Required Documentation; Program Coordination; Review Responsibility
findings.violation: Four sections give unreconciled, apparently competing accounts of who approves a request, the manager, a department-specific approver the benefits team routes to, and the finance office above 200 dollars, with no signal for how the three relate or which one governs, so a reader cannot construct a single picture of what happens to their own request.

findings.evidence: Program Overview: "The people operations office publishes the reimbursement log each quarter." Eligibility: "the home-office equipment stipend become available" then two sentences later "reimbursement is not available without a completed receipt." Heading "Reimbursement Amounts" over the sentence "The stipend pays up to 500 dollars per benefit year." Terminology Notes: "Finance reconciles the stipend item against the request log each month."
findings.fix: Pick one term for the payment (for example, stipend) and one term for the tracking log, and use each consistently throughout, adding a one-line equivalence note if a second term must survive from an earlier draft.
findings.location: Program Overview; Eligibility; Reimbursement Amounts; Terminology Notes
findings.violation: The single payment this policy governs is named stipend, reimbursement, and stipend item interchangeably across sections with no defined-terms statement that they mean the same thing, and the log that tracks it is called both the reimbursement log and the request log, so a reader cannot tell whether these are the same artifact or different ones.

findings.evidence: If the position counts as full-time, the stipend can apply. If the employee has completed 90 days of continuous service, the stipend can apply. If the request arrives before the benefit year ends, the stipend can apply. Only once every condition above is met does the home-office equipment stipend become available to the employee.
findings.fix: State the rule first (for example, the stipend is available once all three conditions below are met), then list the three conditions.
findings.violation: The paragraph opens with three separate conditional sentences before its fourth sentence finally states the governing rule, so the reader has to hold three unresolved conditions in mind before learning what they add up to.

findings.evidence: The two-sentence "Request Steps" section ("Completing the request begins with confirming eligibility, and uploading the receipt.") appears after Approval Timeline, Required Documentation, Reimbursement Amounts, Restrictions and Exceptions, and Terminology Notes, all of which describe what happens once a request already exists.
findings.fix: Move Request Steps immediately after or into How to Apply, before Approval Timeline, so the reader meets the start-to-finish steps before the sections that describe what happens after submission.
findings.location: Request Steps section, and its position relative to How to Apply
findings.violation: The section stating how a request actually begins is placed after five sections that only make sense once a request has already been submitted, so a reader trying to start a request has to read past approval timing, documentation retention, payout amounts, and terminology before reaching the one section that tells them where to start.

findings.evidence: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.fix: Split the sentence at a subordinate-clause boundary.
findings.violation: The sentence runs to 36 words with 4 subordinate-clause markers, longer than the reader can hold in mind on a single pass.

findings.evidence: Then, the review takes longer because the manager who normally handles it is traveling; the backup reviewer who covers for absences was not told that the request needs sign-off before the portal releases the confirmation email.
findings.fix: End the sentence on the fact that explains the delay (the backup reviewer was not told sign-off is required), and move the confirmation-email detail to a separate sentence or drop it.
findings.violation: The sentence's newest and most consequential fact, that the backup reviewer was never told sign-off is needed, sits in the middle, while the sentence closes on a routine procedural detail, when the confirmation email goes out, so the reader's attention lands on the least important part of the sentence instead of the fact that explains the delay.

findings.evidence: The request is reviewed within two business days.
findings.fix: Rewrite the sentence in active voice, naming the actor that performs the action.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a be-verb plus past-participle passive construction in a context where the actor is recoverable and worth naming directly.

findings.evidence: Also, the deposit happens in order to offset costs the employee already paid at this point in time.
findings.fix: Replace the wordy phrase with its plain equivalent (for example, because for due to the fact that).
findings.violation: The sentence uses a wordy construction from the fixed wordy-phrase list that a shorter equivalent would carry with no loss of meaning.

findings.evidence: However, reimbursement is not available without a completed receipt.
findings.fix: Restate the sentence with at most one negation, or recast it as a positive statement.
findings.violation: 2 negation markers from the fixed negation list co-occur in one clause, so the reader has to work out the statement's logical sign before understanding it.

findings.fix: Replace the heading with text specific enough to be found by scanning.
findings.violation: The heading text matches the fixed list of non-specific heading labels, so a reader scanning headings cannot tell whether the section applies to them.

findings.evidence: The manager approves items pursuant to internal discretion, notwithstanding the standard review checklist.
findings.fix: Replace the jargon term with a plain equivalent, or define it at first use.
findings.violation: The sentence uses a legal or foreign-language jargon term from the fixed list with no plain-language definition in the same or the following sentence.
